exam: A 6‑year‑old presents with ascending weakness after a malaria episode – what is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management? — Recognise Guillain‑Barré; start IVIG/plasma exchange, monitor respiration.

A child has unilateral facial droop including the forehead after a recent viral illness – how does this differentiate Bell palsy from a central stroke? — LMN palsy involves forehead; central lesions spare it; urgent imaging not required if isolated LMN.

You suspect cauda equina syndrome in a 10‑year‑old with saddle anaesthesia – what red‑flag investigations are mandatory? — Urgent MRI of lumbosacral spine; if unavailable, arrange urgent referral for surgical decompression.

A patient with HIV presents with peripheral neuropathy – which investigations confirm an LMN process and guide therapy? — Nerve conduction studies to differentiate demyelinating vs axonal; CSF for opportunistic infections; treat underlying HIV and consider gabapentin for pain.
Why is physiotherapy essential after an LMN lesion, and when can it be started? — Prevents contractures and maintains muscle length; begin as soon as the patient is medically stable.
What laboratory result could falsely reassure you in early Guillain‑Barré, and how should you act? — Normal CSF protein early; repeat lumbar puncture after 7‑10 days if clinical suspicion remains.
A child with severe facial LMN palsy cannot close the eye – what complication must you prevent and how? — Corneal ulceration; use lubricating drops and eye taping.

In a low‑resource setting without EMG, how do you differentiate an LMN lesion from a myopathy? — Look for fasciculations and reduced reflexes (LMN) versus preserved reflexes and proximal weakness without wasting (myopathy).
ai.title: Lower Motor Neuron Lesion
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Lower motor neuron (LMN) lesions cause weakness, atrophy, fasciculations and reduced reflexes. In children, common causes include infections, trauma and hereditary neuropathies, often presenting in low‑resource settings.

b: Weakness affecting the whole muscle, including the forehead in facial palsy
Fasciculations on inspection or with gentle percussion
Reduced or absent deep tendon reflexes
sections.p: An LMN lesion involves damage to the anterior horn cell, peripheral nerve, root or neuromuscular junction, producing flaccid weakness, muscle wasting and hyporeflexia.

b: MRC 0‑2: severe, often needs supportive care
MRC 3‑4: moderate, may ambulate with assistance
MRC 5: near‑normal strength
sections.p: Severity is graded by the Medical Research Council (MRC) scale (0‑5) and by functional impact on feeding, breathing and mobility.

b: Post‑viral peripheral neuropathy (e.g., Guillain‑Barré syndrome after malaria, HIV, or recent viral illness)
Acute bacterial meningitis with cranial nerve involvement
Traumatic nerve root injury (e.g., falls, road‑traffic accidents)
Hereditary neuropathies (e.g., Charcot‑Marie‑Tooth disease)
Nutritional deficiency neuropathy (vitamin B12, thiamine)
Toxin exposure (herbal remedies, organophosphates)
sections.p: In low‑resource African settings the most frequent aetiologies are infectious and traumatic.

b: Ascending weakness in Guillain‑Barré
Saddle anaesthesia and areflexic bladder in cauda equina
Focal facial droop with forehead involvement in Bell palsy
sections.p: Children present with rapid‑onset weakness, difficulty feeding or breathing, and loss of reflexes. Facial LMN palsy shows forehead involvement and inability to close the eye.

t.b: Is the lesion demyelinating or axonal? Shows reduced amplitude (axon loss) or slowed conduction (demyelination).
Is there albuminocytologic dissociation? Elevated protein with normal cell count supports Guillain‑Barré.

t.a: Basic labs (CBC, glucose, electrolytes, HIV, malaria smear)
t.b: Are there systemic infections or metabolic causes? Abnormalities guide specific therapy.
Is there compressive lesion (disc herniation, tumour)? Detects cauda equina or root compression.

b: Rapid progression to quadriplegia
Respiratory compromise requiring ventilation
Areflexic bladder leading to urinary retention
Severe dysphagia with aspiration risk
sections.p: Prompt recognition prevents respiratory failure, permanent paralysis and autonomic dysfunction.

b: IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) or plasma exchange for Guillain‑Barré – chosen for immune modulation; avoid steroids as they do not improve outcomes.
Antibiotics for bacterial meningitis (e.g., ceftriaxone) – early therapy reduces nerve damage.
Physiotherapy and gentle range‑of‑motion exercises to maintain muscle length.
Eye care for facial palsy: lubricating drops and taping to prevent corneal ulceration.
Nutritional support and vitamin supplementation when deficiency suspected.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide supportive care, and prevent secondary complications.

b: Monthly MRC grading until plateau reached
Pulmonary function monitoring in severe cases
Education on safe herbal product use
sections.p: Regular assessment of strength, reflexes and respiratory function is essential. Vaccination and malaria prophylaxis reduce infectious triggers.

b: UMN: spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign – absent in LMN
Myasthenia gravis: fatigable weakness, normal reflexes, ocular involvement without forehead weakness
sections.p: Distinguish LMN lesions from upper motor neuron (UMN) signs and from neuromuscular junction disorders.

b: Early CSF protein may be normal; repeat after 1 week if suspicion persists
Nerve conduction may be normal in very early axonal loss
sections.p: Normal reflexes early in Guillain‑Barré or mild neuropathy may give false reassurance.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe facial weakness with corneal exposure
